Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Objective 2 Deck Contents 3 How to Play 4 How to Win a Trick 5 Scoring 6 Expansion Cards 7 Pirate Powers Objective During each round, you will bid how many tricks you will take. If you are correct, you earn the number of tricks won times 20. If you guess incorrectly, you lose ten points for each trick off the mark you were. Deck Contents Suit Cards 14 Parrot (green) cards 14 Treasure Chest (yellow) cards 14 Pirate Map (purple) cards 14 Jolly Roger (black) trump cards Special Cards 5 Pirate cards 1 Tigress card 1 Skull King card 2 Mermaid cards 5 Escape cards 2 Loot cards (expansion only) 1 Kraken card (expansion only) 1 White Whale card (expansion only) Total: 70 cards (74 with expansions) How to Play Skull King is a trick-taking game played over 10 rounds. In each round, players are dealt a number of cards equal to the round (e.g., 1 card in Round 1, 2 cards in Round 2, etc.) Each player bids how many tricks they expect to take that round. Points are awarded for each trick taken that matches a player's bid, plus bonus points. Incorrectly matching a bid will cause a loss of points. The player with the most points at the end of the game wins. Tie games are a shared victory. Suit Cards In the deck are 4 suits of numbered cards. Each card in each suit is numbered from 1 to 14. Parrots (green), Treasure Chests (yellow), and Treasure Maps (purple) are standard suits. Jolly Roger (black) is the trump (or superior) suit. This suit outranks all other suits. If any numbered suit card is played first in a trick (even a black card), all other players must "follow suit" and play a card from their hand of that same suit. If you have a card of the suit that was led, you cannot play a black Jolly Roger card. But if you do not have a card in the suit that was led, you may play any other suit card (including a black Jolly Roger card). Cards without numbers (mermaids, pirates, etc.) are NOT suit cards and may be played regardless of what was led. Special Cards A special card can be played in any trick, even if you would normally be required to follow suit. Escape (blue): An Escape card loses to all other cards. Pirate (red): Beats all numbered cards (including black Jolly Roger). Pirate cards have no rank among each other. If multiple are played, the player who played the first Pirate card wins the trick. Tigress: The Tigress can be played as either a Pirate card or an Escape card. You must choose when the card is played. Skull King: Beats Pirates and the Tigress, but loses to a Mermaid. Mermaid: Beats all numbered cards but loses to all Pirate cards except the Skull King. If multiple are played, the player who played the first Mermaid card wins the trick. When an Escape or Loot card is led, the next card sets the lead suit to be followed. If no player plays a Suit or other Special card, the player who played first wins the trick. The Mermaid, Pirate, Skull King, Kraken, and White Whale have no suit. When these are led, each player may play any card they choose. How to Win a Trick If all cards played are the same suit, the player who played the highest numbered card in that suit wins the trick. If a black card was played, the player who played it wins the trick, since it beats any standard suit card. If more than one black card was played, the player who played the highest numbered black card wins the trick. If any special card was played, the player who played it wins the trick (see rules on Special cards to see what beats what). community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] It's fine. I was expecting crazier from its reputation, but it's a simple standard trick taker. With lots of flowcharts when you get many of those special trumps interacting. It does feel weird to me, starting at 1 card and ramping up to 10 over the rounds. I guess it's to ease players into bidding, but I've seen other examples of that which are more adventurous (or weirder).

[Rating: 1/10] Game without a game. In reality, you have no influence over anything. The worst game I've played recently.

[Rating: 1.4/10] Un sous-tarot !  Des super atouts, du win to win avec plein d'extra point pour les cartes fortes, un système de pari sans grand intérêt et un système de scoring particulièrement abscons.

[Rating: 2/10] A trick-taking game with a generous helping of uncertainty slathered on top, it’s like playing Hearts in a fog. Calculation is replaced by frustration as the added special cards, whose distribution you have no way to predict, throw random wrenches into your attempts at strategy. You may as well just roll a die and try to guess the number that will come up than play a hand of this.

[Rating: 2/10] Honestly one of my least favorite games. Hate the rip off of Thump with dumb theme rules.

[Rating: 2/10] Simple trick taking with some special characters.  I find the betting system to be unappealing because it's too difficult to determine how many tricks you'll win given the game's design. How can you guess how many tricks you'll win if you have no idea what other people have, and there's no way to change your guess partway through?  I feel this is just a simple trick taking gaming with a terrible betting mechanism that feels pointless.

[Rating: 2/10] [Played once]  A "Wizard" clone that is worse than the (already lackluster) original.

[Rating: 2/10] Too many special cards make this game chaotic. It's a challenge to remember which card beats which other card, so we're always having to check the (nice) reference cards. We like Wizard better. There's a touch of chaos in Wizard but we feel more in control. Sold it.

[Rating: 2/10] Literally always the same. So, even if it works, why should I play it? Why should I BUY it?

[Rating: 3/10] FIRST IMPRESSION:  I see no reason to play this over other traditional card games. Reminds me quite a bit of "Up and Down the River" which was a traditional card game played growing up where hand size increased by one each round and your points depended on whether you made your bid. There's a bit more here but not enough to interest me in another go.

[Rating: 3/10] I initially liked it because it was the only trick-taking game that I knew in which you could bet on how many tricks you'd win.  However, the game is way too long and scoring can be very swingy.  I'd rather play something else like Cat in the Box.

[Rating: 3/10] UPDATE: June 2022  :star::star::nostar::nostar::nostar:  Downgrade to two star. More complicated yet doesn't add enough depth to justify the added rules weight.  =============================  Good trick taking game. The best thing about this, that sets it apart from other trick taking games is that you bet on how often will you win in a round. Which makes it a more challenging play, rather than randomly having the right type of cards.

[Rating: 3/10] Feel like I've played this more than once. Just another trick taking game with powers. Save your money and buy a deck of cards and you'll have a less luck dependent experience. (This is oh hell)

[Rating: 3/10] I love trick taking games and this is one of the most basic and annoying.  Overstays its welcome and requires too much shuffling and scorekeeping.   Oh and it’s just a blatant ripoff of Wizard.  Not sure how this is ranked #62 on the Family list.  Literally any other trick taking game is better.

[Rating: 3/10] I really disliked this game. It seemed to be luck dominated, and required memorization of what certain cards did that sucked any potential fun out of the experience. And on top of all that, it was very ugly.

[Rating: 3/10] 2025-01-20  Initial Rating: 6.0 (January 2025)  • I’m surprised to find out Skull King is from 2013. I thought it was a much more recent release, especially with so many friends raving about it now. Everyone compares it favorably to Wizard, a game I kind of like, but for me, Skull King didn’t meet the hype.  • The pirate theme is lighthearted and pasted on. It is only supported by the great art.  • Skull King is a trick-taking game, and I actively dislike those these days. Gameplay is very reminiscent of Wizard.
